sections.b: Book IV of the Psalter (Psalms 90–106) begins with the only psalm credited to Moses, "the man of God" (Psalm 90:0), right after Psalm 89's lament over the fallen throne of David. It goes back behind the kings to the wilderness: "Lord, you yourself have been our home / in one generation after another" (Psalm 90:1). Then comes the group of psalms that cry "The LORD is King!" (Psalms 93; 95–99), closed by Psalm 100, and Psalm 101, a human king's vow. Many scholars, following Gerald Wilson, read Book IV as the exiles' answer to the end of the monarchy: Israel's true King still reigns. Rabbinic tradition credits Psalms 90–100 to Moses. In Greek and Latin Bibles these are Psalms 89–100.

Nearly all of Psalm 96 appears in the song David's Levites sing when the ark comes to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16:23–33), joined to parts of Psalms 105 and 106. Most scholars think the Chronicler built the song from psalms already in use, adjusting a few words for a time before the temple ("his place" for "his sanctuary"). The site's Plain English Translation gives the two texts the same wording wherever the Hebrew is the same.

common: Psalms 93 and 95–99 form a group celebrating the LORD as King.
uncommon: Some scholars think the kingship psalms were sung at a yearly festival of God's enthronement (Mowinckel).

sections.h: "The LORD is King!" in the Psalms
sections.b: The cry YHWH malakh, "The LORD is King!", opens Psalms 93, 97 and 99 and stands at the center of Psalm 96:10. These psalms praise the King as Creator who has set the world firm (Psalm 93:1), as "a great King over all the gods" (Psalm 95:3), as the holy one enthroned on the cherubim in Zion (Psalm 99:1), and as the Judge who "is coming to judge the earth" (Psalm 96:13). The kingdom here is not a territory but God's rule over every nation and every chaotic power, now and to come. Jewish liturgy kept these psalms together in the Friday evening service; Christians hear in them the kingdom Jesus proclaimed.
sections.refs: Psalm 93:1–5; Psalm 95:3; Psalm 96:10–13; Psalm 97:1–2; Psalm 99:1–5; Mark 1:15

common: The kingship psalms celebrate God's present rule and look forward to its full coming.
uncommon: Some scholars read "YHWH malakh" as "the LORD has become King," a cry at a festival of enthronement.

sections.b: Psalm 94 opens: "God who takes vengeance, LORD, / God who takes vengeance, shine out!" (Psalm 94:1). The singer does not curse his enemies by name or ask to take revenge himself. He hands judgment to the "Judge of the earth" (Psalm 94:2), against rulers who crush widows, foreigners and orphans and make misery into law (Psalm 94:5–6, 20). The psalm ends in confidence: "He has brought their wrongdoing back upon them" (Psalm 94:23). It draws on Deuteronomy 32:35, the verse Paul quotes when he tells believers not to avenge themselves (Romans 12:19).

sections.h: Psalm 92: a song for the Sabbath day
sections.b: Psalm 92 is the only psalm whose Hebrew title assigns it to a day: "A psalm. A song for the Sabbath day" (Psalm 92:0). The Mishnah says the Levites sang it at the Sabbath offerings (Tamid 7:4), and it still closes Kabbalat Shabbat. Its theme is praise for God's works and trust in his justice. The Targum says Adam sang it on the first Sabbath, and the Mishnah calls it a song for the age to come, "the day that is all Sabbath."

sections.h: Psalm 95 and Hebrews 4: the rest that remains
sections.b: Psalm 95 ends with God's oath that the wilderness generation would never come into his place of rest (Psalm 95:11). Hebrews joins that verse to Genesis 2:2, God's rest on the seventh day, and concludes that a Sabbath rest still remains for God's people, entered by faith (Hebrews 4:1–11). Christians have drawn different conclusions about the weekly day from this passage: see Psalm 95's chapter page.

In Psalm 95:11 God swears that the generation who tested him in the wilderness "will never come into my place of rest." In Deuteronomy the rest is the land and the place God chooses (Deuteronomy 12:9), and Psalm 132:8 and 132:14 call the temple his resting place. Hebrews 3–4 reads the oath as pointing past both to God's own seventh-day rest, still open "today" to those who believe (Hebrews 4:3–10).

sections.h: Moses in Book IV of the Psalms
sections.b: Moses is named eight times in the Psalms, seven of them in Book IV. Psalm 90 is "A prayer of Moses, the man of God" (Psalm 90:0), echoing Deuteronomy 33:1. Psalm 99:6 remembers him with Aaron and Samuel as one who called on God and was answered. Psalms 103, 105 and 106 recall his work in the exodus and wilderness. Rabbinic tradition credits Psalms 90–100 to him, eleven psalms for the eleven tribes he blessed.
sections.refs: Psalm 90:0; Psalm 99:6; Psalm 103:7; Psalm 105:26; Psalm 106:23; Deuteronomy 33:1

sections.b: Psalm 91 uses the picture of a bird sheltering its young: "With his long feathers he will cover you over; / beneath his wings you can take shelter" (Psalm 91:4). The image goes back to Deuteronomy 32:11 and Ruth 2:12. Rashi reads it as shelter under the wings of the Shekhinah, and Jesus uses it of himself over Jerusalem (Matthew 23:37).

sections.h: Psalm 91:11: "he will give his angels orders"
sections.b: Psalm 91:11 promises the one who trusts God: "For he will give his angels orders about you, / to guard you on every road you take." The devil quotes 91:11–12 to Jesus at the temple's pinnacle (Matthew 4:6; Luke 4:10–11). The verse is the main Old Testament text for the guardian angel in Catholic and Orthodox teaching; Reformed teachers accept angelic protection but not a single assigned angel (see Psalm 91's chapter page). Hebrews 1:14 calls angels spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation.

In the temptation story the devil uses Scripture: he quotes Psalm 91:11–12 to invite Jesus to throw himself from the temple (Matthew 4:5–7; Luke 4:9–12). Jesus answers with Deuteronomy 6:16. The next verse promises that the one who trusts will "stamp down" the serpent (Psalm 91:13), a line Christians have linked to Genesis 3:15.

sections.h: The throne in the kingship psalms
sections.b: The kingship psalms describe God's throne: "Your throne has stood firm from the start" (Psalm 93:2); "his throne rests on righteousness and justice" (Psalm 97:2, echoing Psalm 89:14); "He sits on the cherubim as his throne" (Psalm 99:1), with the ark as "the footstool for his feet" (Psalm 99:5). Psalm 94:20 sets against it a human "throne that brings ruin," which cannot be joined with God.
sections.refs: Psalm 93:2; Psalm 97:2; Psalm 99:1; Psalm 99:5; Psalm 94:20; Psalm 89:14

sections.b: In Psalm 93 the rivers lift up their voice three times, but "the LORD on high" is mightier than the roar of the vast waters (Psalm 93:3–4). The sea is the old picture of chaos, as in the Canaanite story of Baal's victory over Prince Sea and Judge River. Here the waters are not killed; they are simply outmatched. In Psalms 96:11 and 98:7 the same sea is called to roar in praise.

sections.h: From the tree: Psalm 96:10 in the early church
sections.b: Justin Martyr and Tertullian quoted the line "The LORD is King!" of Psalm 96:10 with the added words "from the tree" (Greek apo tou xylou), and the Old Latin psalters read Dominus regnavit a ligno, sung in Venantius Fortunatus' hymn Vexilla regis. Justin claimed that the Jews had cut the words out. No Hebrew manuscript and none of the great Greek manuscripts have them, and most scholars think they began as a Christian comment. They show how early Christians read the King of the psalm as Christ reigning from the cross (compare Acts 10:39; 1 Peter 2:24).

Some of the best-known English hymns come from these psalms: Isaac Watts' paraphrases "O God, Our Help in Ages Past" and "Joy to the World," from Psalms 90 and 98, and William Kethe's "All People That on Earth Do Dwell," from Psalm 100, sung to the Genevan tune now called the Old Hundredth. Psalm 92 praises God with ten-stringed instrument and lyre (Psalm 92:3), and Psalm 98 with lyre, trumpets and ram's horn (Psalm 98:5–6).

Two psalms of this group open the church's daily prayer. Psalm 95 (the Venite, "Come") is the invitatory psalm of the Liturgy of the Hours and of the Rule of Benedict, and of Morning Prayer in the Book of Common Prayer. Psalm 100 (the Jubilate) is its alternative. Both move from a call to worship to a confession that the worshipers belong to God: "we are the people he pastures" (Psalm 95:7); "his people, the flock he pastures" (Psalm 100:3). Psalm 95 adds the warning: "Today, if you would only listen to his voice!"

Psalm 96:5 calls every god of the peoples "a nothing-god" (elilim), a pun on elohim, "gods," while the LORD made the heavens. Psalm 97:7 shames "everyone who serves a carved image" and "those who boast of nothing-gods," and commands the gods themselves to bow. The Greek translators read elilim as "demons" in 96:5, a reading Paul echoes in 1 Corinthians 10:20.

Psalm 101 follows the psalms of God's kingship with a human king's pledge: to walk with a whole heart inside his own house (Psalm 101:2), to silence slanderers and the proud, to choose the faithful as his servants, and to cut off "from the city of the LORD all who do wrong" (Psalm 101:8). Many scholars read it as a coronation vow. Luther's 1534 exposition made it a mirror for Christian princes.

Moses' prayer asks: "Turn back, LORD! How long? / Change your mind about your servants" (Psalm 90:13). The verb is nicham, the one used when God relented at Moses' plea after the golden calf (Exodus 32:12–14). The psalm's only Mosaic prayer asks God to do again what he did then.

Psalm 95:8–11 recalls the wilderness testing at Meribah and Massah (Exodus 17:1–7) and the forty years after the spies' report (Numbers 14:20–35), as a warning to every later generation: "Do not make your hearts hard." The Greek translates the names as "the rebellion" and "the day of testing," the form Hebrews 3:8 quotes.

Psalm 99:1 says of the LORD: "He sits on the cherubim as his throne." The phrase recalls the cherubim on the ark's cover (Exodus 25:22) and the title "the LORD of Armies, who sits on the cherubim as his throne" (1 Samuel 4:4). In Psalm 99:5 the ark is the footstool before the invisible throne.
